twelfth noun

the Roman twelfths and their names

also a twelfth, one twelfth, twelfths, two twelfths, three twelfths, four twelfths, five twelfths, six twelfths, seven twelfths, eight twelfths, nine twelfths, ten twelfths, eleven twelfths, a sixth, two thirds, five sixths, duodecimal fractions, fractions of the as, ounce (a twelfth)

classical

Cic. Att. 13.48.1: Caesar, opīnor, ex ūnciā
Hor. Ars 327
Traupman 355

1ūncia: long u (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). Bennett §52: “like ūnus”, from which Varro derives it (ūncia ab ūnō, LL 5.171; de Vaan s.v. ūnus). The Romance words (Italian oncia, Spanish onza) point to a short vowel in later Latin; Rosen, Language 40 (1964) 21–22, takes *oiniciā through *ūnciā, with a later shortening.

ūncia1, ūnciae f.

noun, first declension

one twelfth

The Romans divided the as, and anything else they counted in twelfths (an inheritance, a pound, a foot, an acre, interest, the hour), by these names. Each larger name counts ūnciae: quīncūnx and septūnx are “five” and “seven ounces”, dōdrāns, dēxtāns and deūnx are the as less a quarter, a sixth and an ounce. On the bronze coins of the Republic the sēmis is marked S and each ūncia a pellet. On the clock each twelfth of the hour is five minutes: see “telling the time”.

Other words

  • sextāns, sextantis m. — two twelfths, a sixth

    noun, third declension · classical · Liv. 2.33.11: extulit eum plēbs sextantibus conlātīs in capita

  • quadrāns, quadrantis m. — three twelfths, a quarter

    noun, third declension · classical · Gell. 3.10.11: pedēs duodecim et quadrantem

  • triēns, trientis m. — four twelfths, a third

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Att. 13.48.1: Lepta ex triente; Hor. Ars 328

  • 2quīncūnx, septūnx, deūnx: long u, from ūncia (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). Bennett §52 (each “from ūncia”) and §42.4, where the compounds in -ūnx are among the exceptions to his rule that a third-declension word ending in two consonants has a short vowel. deūnx keeps the short de- before a vowel (Lewis & Short dĕ-unx).

    quīncūnx2, quīncūncis m. — five twelfths

    noun, third declension · classical · Hor. Ars 327

  • sēmis, sēmissis m. — six twelfths, a half

    noun, third declension · classical · Plin. NH 18.35: sex dominī sēmissem Āfricae possidēbant; Hor. Ars 330

  • septūnx2, septūncis m. — seven twelfths

    noun, third declension · classical · Col. 5.1.11 (of an acre); Liv. 23.19.16 (seven ounces of gold)

  • bēs, bessis m. — eight twelfths, two thirds

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Att. 4.15.7: faenus ex triente … factum erat bessibus

  • dōdrāns, dōdrantis m. — nine twelfths, three quarters

    noun, third declension · classical · Nep. Att. 5.2; Plin. NH 18.219: dōdrāns hōrae

  • 3dēxtāns: long e (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). From dē + sextāns, the as less a sixth (Bennett §52; Lewis & Short gives the same derivation). The vowel before ns is long.

    dēxtāns3, dēxtantis m. — ten twelfths, five sixths

    noun, third declension · classical · Suet. Ner. 32; Plin. NH 18.324: dēxtāns hōrae

  • deūnx2, deūncis m. — eleven twelfths

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Caecin. 6 (Lewis & Short): hērēs ex deunce

Examples

  • sī dē quīncūnce remōta est ūncia, quid superat? … — triēns. — eu! rem poteris servāre tuam. redit ūncia, quid fit? — sēmis

    If one twelfth is taken from five twelfths, what is left? — A third. — Well done! You’ll be able to look after your money. Put the twelfth back: what does it make? — A half.Hor. Ars 327–330

  • Pygmaeōs quoque haut longē ab hīs nāscī, quōrum quī longissimī sint, nōn longiōrēs esse quam pedēs duo et quadrantem

    and that the Pygmies are born not far from them, the tallest of whom are no more than two and a quarter feet tallGell. 9.4.11
